passage: Tanvir's Abba bought him a small packet of cream biscuits from the kirana shop below their Bengaluru apartment. There were only four inside. Chandrika from the third floor had none. She looked at the packet, then at her shoes. Tanvir ate one slowly, licking out the cream. It was his favourite kind. He looked at the three left, then at Chandrika. He held one out, pulled it back a little, then held it out again. "One for you," he said. "And the last one we break." He snapped it and gave her the bigger half by mistake. He frowned, but let her keep it.

qa.q: How many biscuits were in the packet?
qa.a: There were only four biscuits inside.

qa.q: What does Tanvir pulling the biscuit back and then holding it out again show?
qa.a: He felt torn between keeping his favourite biscuits and sharing with Chandrika, and his kindness won.

qa.q: How could Abba respond to what Tanvir did?
qa.a: He could tell Tanvir he noticed that sharing a favourite treat was hard and that he did it anyway, so Tanvir values the choice.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel standing there without any biscuits?
qa.a: She probably felt left out and shy, so being offered one likely felt warm and surprising.

grounding: It shows a child sharing a small, favourite treat even though it costs him something he wanted.

passage:
"I need pink for the flower," said Irawati.
Pema hugged the pink crayon. "I need it for my princess."
"But you've had it for ages."
"It's the only pink. And it's my favourite."
Mama called from the kitchen, "What's the fight, girls?"
"No fight," Pema called back. She looked at the crayon, then at Irawati's empty flower. "You can do your flower. Then give it back, okay?"
"Okay. I'll be quick."
"Not too quick. Colour it nicely." Pema handed it over and started on her princess's hair in yellow instead.

qa.q: What colour did Pema use for her princess's hair instead?
qa.a: She used yellow.

qa.q: What does Pema hugging the crayon suggest she felt about sharing it?
qa.a: She hugged it, said it was her favourite and the only pink, and made Irawati promise to give it back.

qa.q: What could Mama say if she walks in now?
qa.a: She might notice aloud that Pema gave up her favourite crayon while she still wanted it, without making a big fuss.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel when Pema tells her to colour it nicely?
qa.a: She may feel trusted and relieved, and more willing to share with Pema next time. 😊

grounding: It shows a young child giving up the only pink crayon to her sister even though she wanted it herself.

passage: Note by Nazia, preschool teacher. At playtime Himani had the only swing that works, the one she waits for all morning. A new girl stood near the pole, holding the chain of the broken swing. Himani swung three times, slowed, and swung again. Then she dragged her feet and stopped. "You can have five swings," she told the new girl, and counted them aloud for her, frowning a little on the last two. Afterwards she got her turn back. I told her I had noticed. Tomorrow I will ask for the other swing to be fixed. 😊

qa.q: How many swings did Himani offer the new girl?
qa.a: She offered her five swings.

qa.q: What does Himani frowning on the last two counts suggest?
qa.a: She was eager to get her turn back and found giving up the swing hard, even while choosing to share it.

qa.q: Why is Nazia's plan to fix the other swing useful?
qa.a: With two working swings, children won't have to give up so much, so sharing can feel lighter and fairer.

qa.q: What was it like for the new girl standing by the broken swing?
qa.a: She was probably unsure and left out, so Himani's offer made her feel welcome.

grounding: It shows a child sharing the only working swing with a newcomer despite wanting it herself.

passage: Under the mango tree near the village pond, Preeti had two ripe guavas from her Nani's tree. She had been saving them all afternoon. Yamini came and sat beside her, looking. Preeti held both guavas close to her chest and bit her lip. Then she sighed and held one out. 'You take this. It's the smaller one.' She paused. 'No, take the big one.' They ate side by side, slurping.

qa.q: Where did Preeti's guavas come from?
qa.a: They came from her Nani's tree.

qa.q: What does Preeti biting her lip and holding the guavas close suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she really wanted to keep both and felt torn about giving one away.

qa.q: How could Nani encourage Preeti's sharing without forcing it?
qa.a: She could notice it later and say it was kind, letting Preeti feel the good of sharing on her own.

qa.q: What might Yamini feel when Preeti hands her the big guava?
qa.a: She would likely feel surprised and happy, and closer to Preeti. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a young child sharing a limited treat despite wanting it herself, in a village.

passage: In their Vancouver kitchen, only one cookie was left in the tin. Chen grabbed it first. His sister Leila's face fell. Chen looked at the cookie, then at her. He held it up and turned it round. 'I really wanted this,' he said slowly. Then he snapped it in half. One half was bigger. He held both out. 'You pick.' Leila took the smaller piece and smiled.

qa.q: How many cookies were left in the tin?
qa.a: Only one cookie was left.

qa.q: How was Chen feeling when he said 'I really wanted this' before breaking the cookie?
qa.a: He felt torn between wanting the cookie for himself and wanting to share with Leila, which made the choice hard.

qa.q: Which part of Chen's choice was especially fair?
qa.a: Letting Leila pick her half gave her a real choice, which is a kind and fair way to split a treat.

qa.q: How might Leila see her brother after this?
qa.a: She may feel he cares about her, since he gave up something he wanted.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a limited treat even though he wanted it for himself, in Canada.
